title: Infertility after Abortion
text:
Trichopoulos and colleagues studied whether induced and spontaneous abortions increase the risk of secondary infertility (Trichopoulos et al. 1976). Each of 83 infertile women (the cases) was matched with two fertile women (the controls) of the same age, parity and education. One set has a single control. The data are R’s infert, and they ship with the module: in jamovi, Open ▸ Data Library ▸ Conditional Logistic Regression ▸ Infertility after abortion. Or download infert.csv.

Ignoring the matching shrinks both odds ratios to less than half, because the matching factors are related to the exposures. text:
These data are simulated, so that the true odds ratios are known. They mimic a case-control study nested in a cohort. For each of 200 people who developed a disease (the cases), four controls were drawn from the members of the cohort of the same sex and age group who were still free of it. In some sets only two or three suitable controls were found. Download nested.csv.

text:
Step 3: what the matched-set table tells
The table above shows the variable matching ratio: 148 sets with four controls, 34 with three and 16 with two. The conditional likelihood handles any mix of ratios: no weighting or special option is needed.
It also shows 2 sets with no case. In those sets the case has no coffee value, so the case’s row is dropped. The controls left behind have nobody to be compared with, and those sets contribute nothing to the estimates. Whenever the table shows sets with 0 cases or 0 controls, check the missing values of the case and controls in those sets. If the variable with missing values is not needed, leaving it out of the analysis brings those sets back.

title: The Method
text:
Matching makes cases and controls alike on the matching factors, which removes their confounding by design, and the design has to be carried into the analysis. The model behind a matched study gives each matched set \(i\) its own baseline odds of being a case:
\[
\operatorname{logit} P(Y_{ij} = 1) = \alpha_i + \boldsymbol{x}_{ij}^\top \boldsymbol\beta,
\]
where \(j\) indexes the subjects of set \(i\) and \(\boldsymbol\beta\) holds the log odds ratios of interest. The \(\alpha_i\) absorb everything shared within the set: the matching factors and whatever else they stand for.
Two analyses look natural and are both wrong:

Ignoring the matching (an ordinary logistic regression of case status on the exposures) drops the \(\alpha_i\). When the matching factors are related to the exposure, which is why they were matched on, the estimate is usually biased towards the null.
Adding one indicator per matched set to an ordinary logistic regression estimates every \(\alpha_i\). But there are as many of them as sets, each from a handful of subjects, and the maximum likelihood estimate of \(\boldsymbol\beta\) is not consistent in this setting (Andersen 1970). For pairs (1:1) it converges to \(2\boldsymbol\beta\): the odds ratio is squared (Breslow and Day 1980).

title: The Method
text:

\[
\operatorname{logit} P(Y_{ij} = 1) = \alpha_i + \boldsymbol{x}_{ij}^\top \boldsymbol\beta,
\]
where \(j\) indexes the subjects of set \(i\) and \(\boldsymbol\beta\) holds the log odds ratios of interest. The \(\alpha_i\) absorb everything shared within the set: the matching factors and whatever else they stand for.
Two analyses look natural and are both wrong:

Ignoring the matching (an ordinary logistic regression of case status on the exposures) drops the \(\alpha_i\). When the matching factors are related to the exposure, which is why they were matched on, the estimate is usually biased towards the null.
Adding one indicator per matched set to an ordinary logistic regression estimates every \(\alpha_i\). But there are as many of them as sets, each from a handful of subjects, and the maximum likelihood estimate of \(\boldsymbol\beta\) is not consistent in this setting (Andersen 1970). For pairs (1:1) it converges to \(2\boldsymbol\beta\): the odds ratio is squared (Breslow and Day 1980).

title: The Method
text:
The conditional likelihood
The way out is to condition on what each set contributes to the design: the number of cases it contains. For a set with one case (subject 1) and \(M\) controls, the probability that the case is the subject it is, given that exactly one of the \(M+1\) is a case, is
\[
L_i(\boldsymbol\beta) = \frac{\exp(\boldsymbol{x}_{i1}^\top \boldsymbol\beta)}
{\sum_{j=1}^{M+1} \exp(\boldsymbol{x}_{ij}^\top \boldsymbol\beta)}.
\]
The \(\alpha_i\) cancel. The conditional likelihood is the product of the \(L_i\) over the sets, and maximising it gives consistent estimates of \(\boldsymbol\beta\) however many sets there are (Breslow et al. 1978). With \(k\) cases in a set the denominator runs over all \(\binom{M+k}{k}\) ways of choosing \(k\) subjects from the set.

The same likelihood as a stratified Cox model
\(L_i\) has the form of the partial likelihood of a Cox model at a single event time: the case is “the one who failed” and its set is the risk set. So a conditional logistic regression is a Cox model stratified by matched set, in which every subject has the same follow-up time and the cases are the events. With several cases per set they are events tied at that time, and the exact treatment of ties is exactly the conditional likelihood above (Gail et al. 1981). That is what R’s survival::clogit does, and what this module does:
coxph(Surv(rep(1, n), case) ~ x1 + x2 + strata(set), method = "exact")


Exact or approximate
The Likelihood option of the Matching box chooses how ties are handled:








Option
What it is
When




Exact conditional (default)
the conditional likelihood itself
always correct


Efron approximation
Efron’s approximation to it
sets with many cases, where the exact sum gets slow


Breslow approximation
Breslow’s approximation to it
the same, cruder



With one case per set (1:1 or 1:M matching) there are no ties, and the three give identical results. They differ only when a set holds several cases.
For example, with 60 simulated sets of 2 cases and 4 controls, the log odds ratio of a continuous exposure is (exact), (Efron) and (Breslow): both approximations are attenuated towards zero, Breslow’s more. With a third of each set being cases this is a large share of ties, so keep the exact likelihood unless it is too slow.

title: The Method
section: What can and cannot be estimated
text:
What can and cannot be estimated
Everything shared within a set is absorbed by the \(\alpha_i\), and so:

There is no intercept and no absolute risk. The model estimates odds ratios only. This is why the module has no predicted probabilities, classification table, ROC curve or estimated marginal means: those parts of jmv’s logistic regression need the \(\alpha_i\).
A matching factor has no coefficient. A variable that is constant within every set (the matching variables, or anything determined by them) cancels from \(L_i\). The module leaves its rows empty and says so in a note.
Its interactions with an exposure are estimable. Whether the odds ratio of an exposure changes with age, say, is a within-set contrast. Add the interaction in the Model Builder.
Sets without a case or without a control contribute nothing, because their \(L_i\) equals 1. The Matched Sets table counts them. They arise when missing values remove all the cases or all the controls of a set.

title: The Method
text:
Does it matter? A simulation
The figure shows 200 simulated studies for each matching ratio, with 100 matched sets each. The true odds ratio of a binary exposure is 2 (dashed line), and the matching factor is strongly related to the exposure. Points are median estimates; bars span the quartiles.





















Figure 1: Odds ratio estimates from the conditional analysis, from ordinary logistic regression with one indicator per matched set, and from ordinary logistic regression ignoring the matching.



The conditional estimate is centred on the truth at every ratio. With set indicators the odds ratio is about squared for pairs, and the bias shrinks as more controls are matched to each case. Ignoring the matching biases the estimate towards 1 at every ratio.

title: Conditional Logistic Regression in jamovi
text:
In a matched case-control study each case is compared with one or more controls chosen to resemble it on factors such as age, sex or place of residence. The matched sets are part of the design, and the analysis has to keep them: comparisons are made within sets, never across them. Conditional logistic regression does exactly that. It estimates odds ratios from the contrast between each case and its own controls, and the set-specific baseline risks, which a matched design cannot estimate, drop out of the likelihood (Breslow et al. 1978; Breslow and Day 1980).
The condLogReg module brings this analysis to jamovi. It is a clone of jmv’s Binomial Logistic Regression, with the same model builder, reference levels, fit measures and coefficient tables, plus a Matching Variable that identifies the matched sets. The model is fitted by the conditional likelihood, as a Cox model stratified by matched set: the same fit as R’s survival::clogit (Gail et al. 1981; Therneau and Grambsch 2000).

The rest of the panel is the one jmv users know: Model Builder (blocks of predictors, interactions), Reference Levels, Assumption Checks (collinearity), Model Fit (deviance, AIC, BIC, pseudo R², overall test) and Model Coefficients (omnibus likelihood ratio tests). Descriptives: the matched-set table, and a descriptive table of every variable by case/control status, with its missing values;
Model Coefficients: one row per level, with the reference level at OR = 1 and the odds ratio, its confidence interval and p for the others; univariable beside multivariable odds ratios, a trend test and a forest plot on request;

title: Conditional Logistic Regression in jamovi
text:
What is in this tutorial

Method: why matched data need a conditional analysis, the conditional likelihood, its equivalence with a stratified Cox model, and what can and cannot be estimated.
Reading the output: every table and option of the analysis, how each number is computed, and what changed from jmv’s logistic regression.
Use cases in jamovi: three studies analysed step by step, with their data to download. Two of them ship with the module in jamovi’s Data Library, with a third, simulated one.

title: Conditional Logistic Regression in jamovi
text:
Install
The module is sideloaded from the .jmo files on the repository’s Releases page, one per jamovi series and CPU: in jamovi, Modules ▸ jamovi library ▸ Sideload. It needs nothing beyond the packages bundled with jamovi (jmvcore, R6, ggplot2 and survival).

One test per term. The model is refitted without that term’s columns, and the fit is compared with the full model. A factor with several levels gets a single test on several df. With an interaction in the model, the test of a main effect depends on the reference levels, as in jmv.
In jmv’s logistic regression these tests come from car::Anova. Here they are computed by the module, because car substitutes Wald tests for any model with strata.

One row per level, with the variable named once on the left (the layout of the prognosis module’s Cox regression):

a factor starts with its reference level, OR = 1, set in the Reference Levels box (default: the first level), then one row for each other level, labelled by the level alone and compared with the reference;
a covariate has one row, per unit: the OR for a one-unit increase;
an interaction has one row per coefficient, labelled by the levels involved;
there is no intercept row (see the method).

OR is the odds ratio of being a case (the non-reference level of the dependent variable) rather than a control, within the matched sets. Its confidence interval is a Wald interval, exponentiated (\(\exp(\hat\beta \pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\,\mathrm{SE})\), as confint() gives for clogit), at the level set in Confidence interval (95% by default), and p is the Wald test. On the reference row of a factor with three or more levels, p is the likelihood ratio test of the whole factor, the same as in the omnibus table.
Covariate Scaling, a box like Reference Levels, sets the unit of the odds ratio of each covariate: per unit (the default), per 1 SD (the standard deviation on the rows of the model, shown in the label), or per 10, per 100 or per 1000 units. The covariate is divided by that amount before fitting, so the OR becomes \(\mathrm{OR}_{\text{unit}}^{\,c}\) for a scale \(c\), with its interval scaled alike. The p-values, the likelihood ratio tests and the fit measures do not change. Univariable odds ratios, interactions and the forest plot use the same units.
The options of Model Coefficients:

Univariable and multivariable adds the odds ratios of each variable alone (Univariable) beside those of the model (Multivariable). Both are estimated on the same rows, those complete for every variable of the model, so the difference between them is the adjustment alone.
Trend test (factors with 3+ levels) adds p trend on the reference row: the factor replaced by scores 1, 2, 3, … in the order of its levels (Wald test of the score). The univariable trend uses the factor alone, and the multivariable trend keeps the other variables of the model. The scores follow the order of the levels in the data, whichever level is the reference, so order the levels before testing. There is no trend test for a factor that is part of an interaction.
Log odds ratio, SE and Z adds the estimate \(\hat\beta\) (the log odds ratio), its standard error and \(Z = \hat\beta / \mathrm{SE}\) at the right.

Variance inflation factors from the correlation matrix of the estimated coefficients. For a term with more than one coefficient, such as a factor with three levels, the table gives the generalised VIF of the term as a whole (Fox and Monette 1992), with tolerance = 1/VIF. title: Use Cases in jamovi
text:
Three matched case-control studies, analysed step by step with Analyses ▸ Regression ▸ Logistic Regression ▸ Conditional (Matched). Every table on these pages is computed by the module itself, so the numbers are the ones jamovi shows.



Use case
Design
Shows




Infertility after abortion
real data, 1:2 matching
the basic analysis; a count as a covariate or as a factor; a matching factor has no coefficient, but its interaction does; why the matching must not be ignored


Endometrial cancer and oestrogens
real data, 1:4 matching
the descriptive table with missing values; univariable and multivariable odds ratios with a forest plot; how missing values cost matched sets; a dose-response with its trend test; a loosely matched variable


A nested case-control study
simulated, 1:4 with variable ratio
reference levels of a text factor; blocks to see confounding; uninformative sets from missing values



The data can be downloaded as CSV and opened in jamovi. case is coded 0 (control) and 1 (case). jamovi reads it as a nominal integer with 0 as the first level, so 0 is the reference level and the odds ratios compare cases with controls without changing anything.

title: Endometrial Cancer and Oestrogens
text:
In the 1970s, several studies linked the use of conjugated oestrogens after the menopause to endometrial cancer. In a Los Angeles retirement community, each of 63 women with endometrial cancer was matched with four women without it, living in the same community, of the same marital status and born within one year of the case. The data are a classic of the matched case-control literature (Breslow and Day 1980), available in R as Epi::bdendo. They ship with the module: in jamovi, Open ▸ Data Library ▸ Conditional Logistic Regression ▸ Endometrial cancer and oestrogens. Or download bdendo.csv.
